Uh it's time right? >> Yeah. >> So let me start. So welcome to our last session. Please join in. Find your seat. Can you pick up the clicker? You can pick up the clicker. So [clears throat] I welcome you to the last session on transport on media and uh to start with a real uh real surprise for those who didn't invest in space X we are going to space with quick now so welcome Natalia for her talk >> yes thank you for the introduction so hi everyone I'm Nata Proski I'm also from the technical university of Munich and I'm here to present our work on quick and space initial measurements and analysis. So reliable communication is of course always critical but it's especially critical for space missions. There are however there are some challenges that we face when we are communicating in space that we do not encounter on terrestrial networking. Amongst those not not extensively for example intermittent connectivity uh and high latency due to orbit mechanics and low data rate and asymmetrical links due to technical limitations. The current approach to deal with these challenges is the bundle approach which is pioneer being pioneered by the DTN working group here the ITF. However, in recent years and sort of older or another approach has resurfaced and that is to ask the question whether we can deploy the IP stack in space and with it quick. This this topic is being dealt with by the tiptop working group at the ITF and is also what I'm dealing with in my research specifically. I'm trying to answer the question how well do quick implementations perform in space. So uh ah okay so quick itself is the focus of the tiptop working group and this is also why we are focusing on quick and it has already proven its viability in initial simulations. >> We want to look at quick as well as two uh protocol extensions how well they might affect um communication in space notably the act frequency protocol extension and the careful resume protocol extension. Act frequency allows us to delay acknowledgements um which should be at least in theory uh beneficial on highly asynchronous links which is the case for space communications for space links um uh other work which I'm yeah referencing here uh has already proven that this protocol extension is useful for gear connections and in order to uh delay these acknowledgements we can play around or vary two variables notably the max act delay and the act threshold. Sodmax act delay denotes how long we have to wait between or we are allowed to wait between uh yeah two acknowledgements and the act threshold tells us how how many act eliciting packets can be received before an act is issued. Another the other protocol extension we want to look at is the career resume extension. Um this protocol extension allows us to cache congestion control parameters notably the congestion window and the RT in order to shorten the slow start phase um occur for an recurring connection which also in theory should be beneficial for space links. Uh in order to meaningfully evaluate this we will do a statistical evaluation which I will be explaining in just a second. So for measurements as you probably are aware there's a lot of quick implementations out there. We had to focus on two um or we wanted to focus on two notably Quinn and Keys. You can see the concrete uh version numbers on the slide here. Both are written in Rust and we built our own workbench which is based on netm and Linux name spaces and looks as you can see here on the slide. So we have a client and a server communicating over a singular bottleneck link to these bottleneck link uh certain parameters are applied which you can see written here as well. So for the data rate we assume 25 megabit per second. The rationale behind this value is that this is the value of the inter satellite link of the uridium satellites. Then we play around with the delay values which we set to 0.5 1.5 and 3 seconds which translates to an RT of 1 3 and 6 seconds. The rationale behind these values is that we want to focus on communication to the moon and slightly beyond as this is also the focus of the tiptop working group. And for the limit, we set the BDP of the link. Um, where we also calculate any outage durations where we take it into the calculation here as well, which of course is only possible since we know in advance how long any outages are going to be and which is obviously not quite too realistic. [snorts] So I already mentioned that we want to look at the protocol extensions. Um but another topic that we also want to focus on in our evaluations are the outages due to the intermented connectivity. For this we had to introduce two new metrics. First we had to introduce the stability metric um in order to determine when a connection would reach a sort of stable state after the slow start in the beginning of the connection. The reason we wanted to do this is we wanted to have outages occurring in the stable state and well to know when this happened we had to introduce this metric. So I'm not going to go too much into detail how exactly this is being done because that would need a longer explanation which you can see in the paper. But we assume a connection to be stable once the throughput says relatively consistent over a period of time. And then in order to understand whether or not a connection has recovered from an outage we also need a recovery metric. For this we compare the congestion window just before um and after the outage in a jumping window of 10 times RT. So we calculate the average congestion window in this time period which we then refer to as the target congestion window and then calculate it after the outage as well which and once the congestion window in these jumping window sizes has reached the target congestion window we understand the connection to have recovered. We translate this or we understand this as the both the recovery percentage which is simply the fraction of this recovered congestion window and a target congestion window as well as the recovery time stamp um which is simply how long it took to reach um yeah any a recovered state after an outage and it's always relative to the end of the last outage. In case no recovery was observed, which we're going to see in just a second, we denote this value to B minus one. In order to have some sort of confidence in our results, we evaluated this over three different runs and calculated both the mean and the standard deviation values of both the recovery percentage and the recovery time stamp of which I will only be presenting the mean value here in this presentation. So moving on to our to the results. Um first we played around with the AR frequency protocol extension. This is also the only uh scenario where we actually use asymmetrical links notably with a factor of 10 meaning that the down link had a data rate one/10enth uh of the uplink. However, even though we played around with both the max A delay and the requested MAC um maximum AK um delay an act threshold, sorry. Um we could not find any significant improvements in the flow completion times when using this protocol extension which is also the reason why we only uh tested this in Quinn where it was already implemented and did not implement or evaluate it in kiche. Moving on to the careful resume protocol extension. Here I already mentioned earlier that we conducted a statistical evaluation. This means that we had uh 10 baseline runs which did not use the protocol extension but simply cached the values and then 10 careful resume um runs which use the protocol extension with the um parameters that we had just cached in the baseline runs. And here you can see the results on the slide here as well. So we could see some improvements for the flow completion time for kish. However, not really for Quinn. Um for Quinn it was especially surprising that BBR how that the flow completion time of BBR actually worsened when using the careful resume protocol extension. However, we chocked that up to an implementation error since in previous or yeah sort of uh very initial um evaluations this was not the case and so we chocked this up in this case to simply an implementation error which we will have to fix. Moving on to our outages here we evaluated both singular and multiple outages which you will see on the next slide um and yeah represented it in heat map heat maps. So here you can see um in each field you can see the in the color the recovery percentage which is always the average recovery percentage over the three different runs and um the time stamp which is the value written in each field again the average value. So here we can see um that the recovery percentage was more stable for cubic than for Quinn as the colors for the recovery percentage stay closer together for cubic than they do for Quinn uh for BBR. the recovery time stamp uh grows for higher RT which is as expected. However, what is unexpected is that there are some exceptions for an RT of 3 seconds notably for key cubic where this is persistent or consistent. Looking more closer at the values, we can see that the only sort of combination of implementation and congestion control algorithm that struggle to recover is that of quinn and cubic. Um as you can see that that this is the only combination where we can see minus ones in the values for the time stamps. Notably also only for lower RTS which could be kind of s which is kind of surprising. Another sort of oddity we can see for Quinn is that for Quinn BBR we see a very high spike um for an RT of 1 second and an outage duration of 8 seconds. So that yellow fear that you can see down there um which is simply due to how Quinn works and this is this is understandable once you look at the exact uh sending behavior of Quinn that it sends in certain bursts. Moving on before I run out of time we also evaluated uh two outages. So these were again both in the stable state mainly. So the first outage here occurs at the same time as in the previous evaluation and the second outage occurs once the recovered has is understood to be recovered. The exact values for this can be found in the paper. So here we can see that the recovery percentage now stay more stable for Kish rather than for Quinn as again the colors are more closer to each other. Um the recovery time stamp again grows for higher RT which again is as expected but again there are some exceptions for an RT of 3 seconds which in behavior is quite comparable to that of a single single outage. And similar as before cubic struggles with recovery notably now not only for Quinn but also for kiche but for Quinn we can now see that that we do not achieve recovery for higher RTS where we struggle to achieve recovery for lower RTS. This already brings me to the end of my presentation. So we have looked at different protocol extensions and how outages might affect quick quick communications. We saw that the a frequency um protocol extension unfortunately does not seem to be beneficial for deep space links at least not in our evaluations. The careful pro the careful resume protocol extension shows promise um even though there were some oddities that we need to figure out but we chucked it up to implementation details. Um, regarding outages, we could see that cubic struggles with outages, especially in Quinn, which is quite expected. And we could also see that the recovery timestamps are relatively stable regardless if one or two outages occur, especially if these outages are both in a sort of yeah understood stable state. Thank you very much for your attention. [applause] >> [applause] >> So Gory Fhist thanks ever so much for bringing this. Um I suspect that the bugs and implementation things are a feature of actually testing like this because when we did implementation in cloudflare kiche of careful regime we also saw timing errors that we didn't expect which we traced down to unusual ways in which times were manipulated and also recovery problems. So this is actually stress testing protocols. So, it's a good thing to do experimentation with and I'm really think it's good. Did you ever look at happy eyeballs? >> Do I have >> happy eyeballs and the idea that Quick and TCP might race one another over this sort of path? >> Uh, so sorry. >> Happy eyeballs. >> Happy eyeballs. >> What is that? >> It's like maybe we'll talk about this. >> Yeah, the answer is probably no, but that also might be an interesting thing to stress test. So, thank [laughter] you. Hello. >> Hello. My name is Robert uh from Hop Platner Institute. Um on slide four, you had a little bit of assumptions on uh your bottleneck parameters in starting. Could you elaborate how you got to those? >> Could you repeat that please? I didn't >> um you had assumptions on your bottleneck parameters. >> Uh how did you come to those? Oh um I mean for like what specifically for the the data rate that was again for >> yes for the data rate >> the data rate yeah that's um that's simply the inter satellite link of the data rate of the inter satellite links of the iridium satellites so this was our next best guess it was very hard to find good values to use there and this seemed like a sensible value so that's why we used it here >> all right thank you >> hi Dish from NPI regarding in the uh BBR experiments that you done uh you know that BBR has probing phases like RT probing or bandwidth probing how your outages were were uh covering these probing phases. >> Uh they didn't and they didn't take that into consideration in what exact phase the the uh yeah the BBR currently was. So that wasn't taken into consideration. >> Thank you. You want to come up or? >> Yeah. >> Okay. Okay. >> Who do you want to run the slides? [applause] >> Hi everyone. I'm Daniel. I'm a PhD student and research assistant at the Technical University of Munich. And today I want to talk about how H3 prioritization can enable the cooperative scheduling in mask. So before we start though, uh let's assume that we have a client and server here that are communicating over some kind of legacy protocol that is difficult to extend. And even though we may not be able to extend this protocol directly, what we can do instead is that we introduce a mask proxy through which we then tunnel all of our traffic. And this works because when we operate mask over H3, we end up inheriting a series of capabilities and extensions that are provided by the entire underlying stack. For instance, we may have selected reliability. We can have prioritization mechanisms and even support for multiple transport layer paths at the same time. And what these features here have in common is that they all ultimately rely on some kind of tailored scheduling solution that relies on application specific knowledge that has been that has been provided by the client and yet mask at the moment does not provide a standard way to do so. The case that we want to make today is that the extensible prioritization scheme for HTTP or EPS for short is already in fact capable of providing these missing semantics. EPS uh operates on two parameters. We have U and I where the U stands for the urgency which is a priority that ranges from low to high. And we also have a boolean flag which which essentially uh requests the peer to multiplex its resources. Beyond that we can also introduce new parameters that are able to extend these cap that are able to extend these cap scheduling capabilities as implied by the name. All of which in a mass context and ultimately end up applying to uh data streams and also connect requests. When we looked at related work, we found that both cooperative approaches as well as flow aware scheduling uh were able to provide performance-enhancing services in mask. What was missing though was precisely this uh signaling protocol that enables the client to convey its intent to the proxy which is why in our work here we ended up repurposing EPS to that end. So uh EPS it was very natural to embed these cooperative semantics into EPS because it essentially already has these strict priorities that we see in multipath quick literature. These are covered here by the urgency parameter. The demand that we have for multipplexing in quick and by extension uh H3 and mask uh these are provided here by the incremental flows. Nothing in the specification prevents EPS from applying to multiath topologies either. And by keeping these new extensions that we introduced uh constrained to what we actually control. So namely the client and the proxy here. Uh we don't have to involve the server at all which is um which was a limitation in prior work that we had seen with uh EPS extensions before. To actually then go ahead and evaluate this approach. We uh designed and implemented our own mask implementation which we called mask nata and this it is essentially able to provide a scheduling framework that enables you to evaluate and measure these uh dynamic approaches in a reproducible manner. to do. So, we built it on top of Tokyo Kiche, which is a quick library that made it very easy to essentially implement these reliable and unreliable uh flows that we have in mask as well as shipping with uh this EPS signaling out of the box. Beyond that, we also wanted to experiment with uh multipath quick and there [clears throat] we found a uh draft implementation for the protocol extension already available in the pull request. Our proxy uh is also able of to offer a pluggable scheduling interface which differs from the baseline that we previously had where that proxy was essentially working with a fixed and staticuler for all of its connections regardless of the the preferences that the client actually had. So our contribution was to essentially move uh these scheduling decisions to the connection level and beyond that also to enable the client to request uh a customuler that is being offered uh at the proxy using this new EPS extension there uh which essentially then operates on top of this outer multipath connection. And we also looked through several quick uh schedulers uh from the literature, some of which we were then able to essentially uh modify to accommodate these uh EPS semantics. Uh and that resulted in schedulers that we here call uh EPS aware. We then evaluated this whole idea on top uh of a proper bare metal test bed. So there we had a client, a proxy and a server. uh we had two physical links between the client and proxy which then mapped to these logical paths at the transport layer and the traffic that was flowing was initiated through uh the client which essentially established nine flows u over that proxy uh and the client also set these EPS requests EPS parameters that essentially were understood here by the proxy which in turn divided these endto-end flows that each retrieved a one megabyte file into these groups of low, medium and high priority. And we also set the incremental flag as well as varying uh these scenarios with respect to whether the tunnels were either reliable or unreliable masks. So we were essentially varying the substrate. We also evaluated different path conditions. So we either had identical path properties or heterogeneous conditions where one path was significantly slower. And we of course also evaluated different scheduling approaches including uh NPS aware scheduler as a case study. What our results then showed at a high level is that for one uh with unreliable mask these U and I semantics they are effectively lost. So the flows they were being essentially uh scheduled uh in a manner that uh was evenly splitting the throughput which is in line with the specification though since um according to the specification they should only apply to streams and that brings us to reliable mask where we have a stream as a substrate and there uh the urgency parameter was indeed able to lower the completion time of these prior prioritized flows. So the higher that we set the urgency the faster these flows actually completed and the incremental flag there that we had set it was essentially making sure that we didn't see any blocking issues for these flows that were being sent in a parallel fashion at the same level of urgency. On top of that, our proxy was indeed able to parse this new EPS extension that we introduced, which at the end of the day is what made that on the-fly scheduleuler selection possible. Which is why we see here that even for these unrei unreliable flows where these semantics previously did not apply there we're all we are able to uh yeah select theuler and we ultimately saw that the round robbins strategy for instance performed pretty well uh under these identical path conditions. The roundrobin scheduler however then performed much much worse uh when we actually moved to heterogeneous paths and that's because now one of the paths was significantly degraded in terms of the RT and its rate which uh just goes to show how important it is that we're actually able to dynamically switch away from an underperforming perhaps due to fluctuating network conditions for example beyond that the EPSAware that we had adapted method before we were able to see that it was indeed able to provide new functionality addressing a recommendation in the EPS specification that these methods to address starvation should be implementation specific. And here concretely was what this uh scheduler was doing is that it was effectively able to sometimes yield the sending opportunity of a high priority flow so that these lower priority flows could still make forward progress uh while still maintaining the overall completion order that the client had requested. So this is essentially the behavior of that incremental flag except that we're now able to sometimes skip between these urgency classes. All of this uh however is still very much a prototype. So we do want to move uh our implementation to a more mature uh quick implementation. We want to evaluate this entire setup under more realistic traffic conditions as well next as well as uh not only working with this concrete case study but also testing other scheduling approaches uh that we can make uh EPS aware. One approach that seems promising that we had seen in the literature for example is that we uh take a high priority flow and that we always assign it to the fastest path which should reduce um the occurrences of out of order arrivals for example. Beyond that, at the moment, this extension uh is only yeah doing its job when we actually create a new tunnel. And a more ideatic approach to this to stay a bit more in line with the uh EPS specification would be to leverage the priority update frames that are able to rep prioritize uh flows in according to the EPS specification. And with that uh we already come to the end. So we were essentially able to see that EPS is indeed able to um provide perflow quality of service uh in mask. EPS was also able to enable these cooperative approaches and it does so while still allowing for room to specialize. Taken together, we believe that uh EPS is a suitable signaling scheme for mass scheduling that we would like to see adopted more. Thank you. ANY [applause] [applause] QUESTIONS? >> HI, UH, Lucas Parardu, uh, one of the co-authors on the priorities draft and a mask enthusiast. So, thanks for this work. It's it's real like a mask proxy does have these scheduling issues to deal with and it's especially with the multipath stuff it's really interesting. So for the streams is kind of given if you're in HTTP3 and you implement prioritization at all as a server. Um the thing to remember is kind of the signaling is distinct from the server doing the scheduling and the header say the the priority header is like one of the inputs into the scheduling decisions the server can make. And in the draft itself is a whole load of text that is trying to guide people towards doing something that's sane for web but that kind of all these caveats and escape mechanisms for doing other stuff. But it was written before we had quick datagramgrams and a kind of mask flow of all of these other multipplex datagramgrams even though quick doesn't model it as a transport service as multipplexed flows. So it's it's very complicated and there's lots of opportunity to do better. So really thanks for doing this research. I posted a link in the chat um about a a way to articulate just datagramgram priorities to try and give a semblance of this different flow linked to those connect requests um as as like similar but slightly different than this might just be worthwhile looking into that to see kind of any any overlaps with those things. Um but yeah just just good work. Thanks. >> Thank you. Yeah, that was a lot to take in. So I would like to connect offline before later on. Uh but we we we did have a bachelor thesis at our chair that uh attempted to do some prioritization on top of datagramgrams as well. Uh so perhaps I could look into that for more uh concrete details on what to do next. Uh but yeah, I do admit that this is all a little bit uh hacky and that we're uh yeah trying to push the boundaries of what EPS is supposed to do. Uh but yeah, I'm open to to feedback on this. >> My my my only comment there is this is this like this whole area is open for improvement. So there's no clear answer. This is why the research is so important to do. Thank you. >> Thank you. >> Yeah. Thank you ever so much. [applause] Okay, looks good. >> Hello, my name is Mart Anglebot. I am also a PhD student at the technical university of Munich and I'm going to present an architecture for multiplexing data channels and media in web RTC using quick and this is work that I've done together with Fabian Funald who's also a student at TUM and my supervisor Jük. So in the last couple of years, Jük and I have also been working on RTP overquick, which is just RTP overquick and no data channels. And that draft is adopted in the AV core working group. Um, it's been in the works for a couple of years now. And it basically defines an application layer protocol that is u mostly an encapsulation format for RTP packets in cri. It supports quicks streams and quick datagramgrams uh for different use cases and it has a so-called flow identifier for multiplexing different RTP streams within a quick connection um or or multiplexing RTP and RTCP in a single quick connection. And the draft also contains some applicability considerations for example for congestion control or for generally sending RTCP over quick. And an interesting use case for RTP over quick is of course WebRTC which is a framework for peer-to-peer real-time media communication on the web. Um WebRTC contains media communication using RGP over UDP usually UDP with a fallback to TCP if UDP is not available. Um and robotc also contains data communication which allows applications to exchange arbitrary data using a protocol called data channels which works on top of SCTP uh and also runs over UDP. Um something that easily happens when applications use both of these at the same time is that um because the different protocols use different congestion controllers these compete with each other for the same bandwidth in the network. So if we have an application sending for example a file transmission over a data channel and we also have a media stream uh running in parallel um something that can easily happen is what we see here is that the media stream receives very little bandwidth while the uh data channel consumes a lot of the bandwidth available in that network. Um and that happens because the SCTP uses usually a lossbased congestion controller uh which also leads to the RTP stream observing a very high jitter as we can see in the bottom graph here. And a solution that has been proposed for this in the past is called coupled congestion control which basically couples the congestion controllers of RTP and SCTP uh to make sure that both of these can get a fair share of the available bandwidth. And I would like to talk about a different alternative architecture using RTP overquick which would use RTP overquick and then multiplex data channels on the same quick connection so that they both use the same congestion controller and share the bandwidth fairly between each other. Um so the traditional architecture in WebRTC looks like this on the left side where we have IP and UDP in the bottom and then we have DTLS on top to secure the RTP streams and SCTP and on top of SCTP we have a data channel protocol and the architecture that we are uh have been working on is this where we have quick as the um transport protocol and on top of that we have RTP um over quick and then uh the same or basically the same data channels protocol but on top of quick instead of um SCTP and uh we can reuse the RTP overquake encapsulation format that we have already defined in the draft I mentioned before. Uh we need a new data channels protocol because we cannot directly transfer the one that we have from SCTP because we need to adapt it to quick.
